Dear Vinita di,
Ammi must have told you I topped the second-semester statistics paper. Please don't make a big deal of it when you call. It genuinely means nothing. The paper was easy, everyone says so, and half the questions were from last year. If it had been hard, I'd have been in the middle like always.
You'll say I'm doing the thing again. Maybe. When I failed the programming practical in first year, I told you it proved I wasn't cut out for engineering. I still think that. So I know it looks odd that the failure counts and this doesn't. But the practical was real. This was a fluke.
Anyway, how is Pune? Is the new flat warm enough?
Rafiq

qa.q: Which paper did Rafiq top?
qa.a: Rafiq topped the second-semester statistics paper.

qa.q: Why does Rafiq insist that topping the paper 'means nothing'?
qa.a: Accepting the success would challenge Rafiq's belief about not being cut out for engineering, so calling the paper easy keeps that belief safe.

qa.q: What question could Vinita di ask to help Rafiq see the pattern?
qa.a: Vinita di could ask why the failed practical counts as 'real' but the topped paper is a 'fluke', and whether both results might count as evidence.

qa.q: How might Vinita di feel reading 'Please don't make a big deal of it'?
qa.a: Vinita di may feel proud but also sad, seeing Rafiq unable to enjoy a real achievement and quick to change the subject.

grounding: Shows a student who tops a paper and calls it a meaningless fluke while treating an earlier failure as real proof about themselves.

passage: Top of the batch, Francis. Me, Samir, first in the design studio jury. You'd think I'd have celebrated. Instead I spent the whole week explaining it away. The jury was tired, they'd seen worse projects that morning, my topic was an easy one, a bus shelter, come on. When my friends took me out for biryani I kept saying, 'Honestly, it's nothing.' But in second year, when one juror called my library model 'confused', I carried that word for months. I told myself that was the real me. The good result was an accident; the bad one was the truth. I only noticed when my mother asked, 'So when do your good marks start counting?' I didn't have an answer. I'm still working on one, if I'm honest.

qa.q: What was Samir's winning project?
qa.a: Samir's topic was a bus shelter.

qa.q: Why did the word 'confused' stay with Samir for months while first place didn't?
qa.a: Samir sees the criticism as 'the real me' and the success as an accident, so bad results fit the self-view and are kept, while good ones are explained away.

qa.q: What turning point did the mother's question create?
qa.a: 'So when do your good marks start counting?' showed Samir the uneven rule, where failures count and successes don't, which is the first step to changing it.

qa.q: How might the friends at the biryani dinner have felt hearing 'it's nothing'?
qa.a: The friends probably felt a little deflated, since they wanted to celebrate, and may have wondered what it would take for Samir to feel proud.

grounding: Shows a student who tops a design jury and explains it away as luck, while keeping an old criticism as the truth.

passage: I'm Kunal, Bhavna's classmate in the M.Sc. chemistry batch. When the results of the thermodynamics paper went up on the notice board, Bhavna's name was at the top, 87 out of 100. People congratulated her in the corridor. She kept saying, 'It was an easy paper, that's all.' It wasn't. Half the class had come out of that exam looking pale; I was one of them. Later, in the canteen, someone asked for her notes and she said, 'Don't, they're not good.' I remember last term, when she got 52 in spectroscopy, she said, 'See, this is my real level.' I can't see inside her head. But from outside, it looks like a bad mark gets to count and a top mark has to come with an excuse.

qa.q: What did Bhavna score in the thermodynamics paper?
qa.a: Bhavna's name was at the top, 87 out of 100.

qa.q: Why might Bhavna call the 52 in spectroscopy 'my real level'?
qa.a: Bhavna seems to see herself as ordinary or weak, so a low mark feels like confirmation while a high mark feels like a mistake that needs an excuse.

qa.q: What could a friend say to help Bhavna notice the pattern?
qa.a: A friend could gently point out that half the class found the paper hard, and ask why the 52 counts as real but the 87 doesn't.

qa.q: How does Kunal see the gap between the paper and Bhavna's story about it?
qa.a: Kunal, who came out of the exam looking pale, knows the paper was hard, so to Kunal the 'easy paper' story sounds unfair to Bhavna herself.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a student who calls her top mark the result of an easy paper while treating a low mark as her real level.

passage:
Monday: The results for Microeconomics went up on the department board. Akash's name was at the top: 91. Jahnavi hugged him. "Topper!" He shrugged. "The paper was easy. Anyone could've done it. It means nothing."

Thursday: In the Statistics class test, Akash got 14 out of 25. He stood by the window, jaw tight. "See? This is the real me. I'm just not good at this subject."

Jahnavi frowned. "On Monday you said the paper was easy, so the 91 didn't count. Today you're saying the 14 proves you're bad?"

"That's different."

"How?"

He didn't have an answer.

Saturday: Jahnavi texted him a photo of a page from her notebook. Two columns: "Things Akash says don't count" and "Things Akash says prove he's bad." The first column was long. The second had one line.

He didn't reply for an hour. Then: "ok. that's a bit weird. I see it."

qa.q: What did Akash get in the Statistics class test?
qa.a: 14 out of 25.

qa.q: Why does Akash treat the 14 as "the real me" but the 91 as meaning nothing?
qa.a: He already sees himself as not good enough, so failures fit that picture and successes get reclassified as flukes. Whatever happens, the negative view stays safe.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did Jahnavi's two columns work?
qa.a: When Akash saw the two columns side by side and admitted "I see it." Seeing the unfair double standard written down made it harder to deny than hearing it said.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel watching Akash dismiss his 91 and cling to his 14?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably feels frustrated and a little sad that he can't enjoy his success. Her patient columns show she cares enough to help him see it.

grounding: Over a week a student who topped one paper says it meant nothing, then treats a weak test as proof he is bad, until a friend shows him the pattern.

passage:
Zainab, beta, I heard you told your Ammi your first-class result was "just luck". Sit with your Rehana Khala a minute.

When I was twenty, I topped my B.Pharm second-year exams in Hyderabad. Top of the whole college. The principal announced it at assembly. And do you know what I said to everyone? "The paper was easy. They must have marked leniently." Every single time.

Then two months later I failed one practical, because my hands shook with a pipette. And that one, I believed completely. "See, this is who I really am."

Your Nana noticed. He said, "Rehana, you've made a strange rule. When you do well, it's luck. When you do badly, it's the truth. Why is only one of them real?"

I didn't have an answer. I still think about it.

So, Zainab. Was it really luck? Or did you study every night for four months?

qa.q: What did Rehana fail two months after topping the exams?
qa.a: One practical.

qa.q: Why did Rehana believe the failed practical completely but not her topping result?
qa.a: She already doubted herself, so failure seemed to confirm who she was, while success felt like something to explain away. The rule kept her low view of herself safe.

qa.q: What turning point does Rehana Khala hope Zainab will reach with her question?
qa.a: She hopes Zainab will admit the four months of studying earned the result, not luck. Counting that success is the first step to breaking the double standard.

qa.q: How might Zainab's Ammi have felt hearing that the result was "just luck"?
qa.a: Ammi might have felt worried or a bit sad, likely having seen how hard Zainab worked. That may be why the story reached Rehana Khala.

grounding: An aunt recalls how at twenty she dismissed topping her exams as luck but believed one failure completely, and asks Zainab to question the same habit.

passage: Tushar, you say your first-class result doesn't count because the paper was easy. Your Irawati Maasi used to say exactly that. In my second year of B.Com in Nagpur, I came first in the whole university in cost accounting. Do you know what I told everyone? 'The paper was simple. Anybody could have done it.' That same year I failed one tax internal, and that one, I believed completely. I told myself: that is who you really are, the rest was luck. For three years I lived like that. Every good mark was an accident; every bad one was the truth. Then my professor, Mrs Kulkarni, called me to her cabin with the university merit list. 'Irawati, if the paper was so easy, why did four hundred students score lower than you?' I had no answer. I still think of that question.

qa.q: Which subject did Irawati come first in?
qa.a: She came first in the whole university in cost accounting.

qa.q: Why did Irawati believe the failed internal completely but not the first rank?
qa.a: She felt unsure of herself deep down, so the failure matched that self-doubt and felt like the truth, while success felt like an accident.

qa.q: What turning point in the story challenged Irawati's thinking?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni's question, why four hundred students scored lower if the paper was so easy, showed the success was real evidence.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kulkarni see Irawati's result?
qa.a: She saw it as genuine achievement, proved by the merit list, and wanted Irawati to stop dismissing it.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, as a student, she called her top result an easy paper while treating one failure as proof of who she was.

passage: Bhavna had written the semester's Indian history paper after three nights of closing shifts at the bakery near her hostel in Pune, dozing on the bus in between. When the results came, she had the highest mark in the class. Hafsa read it off the notice board twice. 'Topper! On three hours of sleep!' Bhavna shook her head. 'Everyone says the paper was easy. It doesn't count.' 'Who's everyone?' 'People.' That evening, a professor's email said her political science essay needed 'more depth'. Bhavna read it on her bed with the bakery apron still on. 'See,' she said. 'That's the truth. I'm average, and the topper thing was a fluke.' Hafsa sat down beside her. 'So when you do badly, it's because you're average, and when you do well, it's because the paper was easy. You've built a game you can't win.' Bhavna pulled the apron over her face.

qa.q: Why does the essay email feel like 'the truth' to Bhavna?

When the results were pinned outside the department at the Kochi college, Sabina's name was at the top of the company law list: 87 out of 100.

Thomas whooped. "Sabina! First!"
"The paper was easy," Sabina said. "Everyone says so. It doesn't mean anything."
"The class average was 54."
"They probably marked leniently. Or I got lucky with the questions."
Thomas frowned. "Last semester, when you got 58 in taxation, you said it proved you were bad at law."
"Because I am bad at taxation."
"So a 58 is proof, and an 87 is luck?"
Sabina started to answer and stopped. She looked at her name on the list. It didn't feel like hers.
"Say 'I did well'," Thomas said. "Just once. Out loud."
She mumbled it, and felt strangely close to tears.

qa.a: Sabina felt uncomfortable with success, and calling it luck or an easy paper kept her belief that she is bad at law.

qa.a: That she counted a 58 as proof but an 87 as luck, and he asked her to say "I did well" aloud to let the success count.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel when Sabina dismisses the result?
qa.a: Thomas is frustrated and a little sad for her, wanting her to see the success clearly.

I'm Irawati, and in my final year I topped the statistics paper. First in a class of sixty. And I spent the whole week explaining why it didn't count.

"The paper was easy," I told Darshan. "The questions were from last year's guide. Anyone who studied the guide would have got it." When the professor congratulated me, I said, "I got lucky with the questions."

In the same month I got a B in econometrics, and I told everyone, "See, I'm just not good at this."

Darshan finally sat me down in the canteen and drew two columns on a napkin: "Things that count" and "Things that don't". Under "count" he wrote: B in econometrics. Under "don't" he wrote: first in statistics. "That's your system," he said. "Does it look fair?"

It didn't. I kept that napkin in my wallet for a year.

qa.q: How many students were in Irawati's class?
qa.a: There were sixty students in the class.

qa.q: Why did Irawati explain away the top result?
qa.a: Irawati felt uneasy with success, so every win became a fluke while a B felt like proof of not being good.

qa.q: How did Darshan's napkin help Irawati?
qa.a: It showed the unfair system, failures counting and successes not, so Irawati could start letting wins count.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt hearing "I got lucky with the questions"?
qa.a: The professor was probably a little puzzled, having congratulated a real achievement.

grounding: A student looks back on topping a paper and calling it luck while counting a B as proof, until a friend drew the two columns.

passage:
Faculty mentor's note, second-year commerce, by Bhavna
Sabina topped the cost accounting paper this semester, 92 out of 100. When I congratulated her, she said, "The paper was easy this time. It doesn't mean anything." I pointed out that the class average was 58. She said, "Then I got lucky with the questions."
Last month, when she scored 61 in taxation, she told me it proved she wasn't cut out for commerce. I noticed the pattern: every high mark is a fluke, every low mark is proof.
Today I showed her both marks side by side and asked, "Why does the 61 count and the 92 doesn't?" She laughed, uncomfortable. "Because the 61 feels true." "And the 92?" "Feels like a mistake."
What I did next: I asked her to write down three things she did to prepare for cost accounting. We'll look at the list before her next exam.

qa.q: What was the class average in the cost accounting paper?
qa.a: The class average was 58.

qa.q: Why does the 61 feel true to Sabina while the 92 feels like a mistake?
qa.a: Sabina feels unsure of her ability, so a low mark fits what she already believes, while a high mark feels uncomfortable and gets called a fluke.

qa.q: What did Bhavna ask Sabina to do, and why?
qa.a: Write down three things she did to prepare, so she can see the 92 came from her own effort, not luck.

qa.q: How might Sabina's classmates see her 92?
qa.a: They would likely see it as a real achievement, since the class average was only 58.

grounding: A mentor notes a student who tops a paper but calls it easy and a fluke, while treating every lower mark as proof.

Wednesday night
Results came out. I topped the statistics paper. 88. Tarun came running to tell me, and everyone was saying "well done, topper".
All I could think was: the paper was easy. Everyone must have done well. It doesn't mean anything.
Then I checked the list. Second highest was 71. Average was 54. So it wasn't easy for everyone.
And here's the strange part, diary. When I failed the economics quiz in September, I told myself for weeks that it proved I'm not smart enough for this course. I never once said "the quiz was hard". The failure counted. The top mark doesn't.
That's not fair to me, is it?
Tarun said, "Just say thank you." So tomorrow I'll try. I'll say thank you. And I'll write 88 on the first page of my notebook.
Sumit

qa.q: How might Tarun feel about Sumit brushing off the result?
qa.a: Tarun seemed excited for Sumit and would probably feel frustrated that the achievement is being dismissed.

grounding: A student's diary shows topping a paper and calling it easy, while an earlier failed quiz was taken as proof, and noticing that double standard.

The results went up on the notice board of the Sangrur college the week before Lohri, and Avni's name sat at the top of the economics list. Deepika, who rode the same bus from the village, spotted it first and shook Avni's arm. "First! In the whole year!"
Avni shrugged, pulling her shawl tighter against the fog. "The paper was easy. Everyone must have got good marks."
"I got fifty-two," Deepika said.
"Then the checking was loose."
On the bus home, past carts stacked with sugarcane, Avni went quiet, then brought up the maths test in October where she had scored badly. "That one shows where I really stand."
Deepika stared. "So the bad one counts and the good one doesn't?"
Avni looked out of the window and didn't answer.
